summary: Pupils aged 9–10 learn that information can be carried as patterns, and that coding is an engineering design task: invent a code, transmit a message as a light or sound pattern, have a partner decode it, and compare competing codes against explicit criteria (speed, distance, reliability in noise, ease of learning). The central experience is encode-THEN-decode with a partner using a shared key, so that 'communication needs an agreed code' is felt rather than told. A concrete→abstract progression (Morse → black/white pixel grids → everyday signals) builds toward the big abstraction that, when combined into longer patterns, any two distinguishable states can represent any message (letters, numbers or pictures), and toward the engineering habit of comparing multiple solutions rather than hunting for one 'right' answer.
misconceptions: Confusing the MESSAGE with the CODE — not seeing that the same message can be sent by many different codes, and the code is a shared SYSTEM of patterns, not the message itself.

Thinking any noise or flash 'communicates' — missing that communication needs an AGREED code both sender and receiver know (carried from the build-a-device prerequisite); an unshared key means no message gets through.

'More complex or longer codes are better' — not grasping efficiency/trade-offs (good codes give frequent symbols short patterns; the best solution depends on the criteria, e.g. speed vs noise-resistance).
Treating binary as mysterious 'computer magic' — rather than simply two distinguishable states used as a pattern; any two different things work.
Not seeing that pictures, numbers and text can ALL be reduced to patterns of two symbols — the core abstraction of digital representation.
Assuming there is one 'right' code — rather than multiple candidate solutions to be compared against criteria and constraints (the engineering-design point of the standard).

activities.title: Invent a code and send it across a gap
steps: Assign your own patterns — flashes/taps, long/short, or 0s and 1s — to letters to DESIGN a code, and write down the key.
Encode a short message (e.g. your name, or 'HI') and send it to a partner across the room as a flashed-torch or tapped-drum pattern.
Have the partner decode it using a copy of the SAME key; then try sending to someone who does NOT have your key and see what happens.
Swap roles so both partners encode and decode at least once.
activities.insight: A message only arrives if both sender and receiver share the same agreed code: a successful decode shows the shared system is working, while a garbled decode may come from a missing or mismatched key or from a sending problem (e.g. long/short or on/off states hard to tell apart). The meaning lives in the agreement, not in the dots/flashes themselves.

activities.title: Pictures are patterns too: the black/white pixel grid
steps: Decode a grid of 0s and 1s (by an agreed convention here 0 = white, 1 = black) by colouring the matching squares, and watch a picture emerge.
Draw your OWN small black/white picture on a grid (e.g. a 5×6 letter 'C'), then write the binary digits for each pixel.
Hand your binary to a partner and have them rebuild the picture from your digits alone.
Discuss: if you wanted more than two colours per pixel, what would you need to add?
activities.insight: A picture can be reduced to a grid of two-state pixels, so images, numbers and text can all be represented as patterns of two symbols. With one binary digit a pixel can only be two colours; more colours need more digits per pixel. Which digit stands for black is an agreed convention, not a fixed fact — the same point the whole topic makes.

activities.title: Compare competing codes against criteria
steps: Build a comparison table: rows are codes (your invented code, Morse, semaphore, a simple on/off code, a drum rhythm), columns are criteria (speed, distance, resistance to noise, ease of learning).
Time how long each code takes to send a typical short message, and note which codes give frequent letters the shortest patterns (e.g. Morse: E = one dot).
Introduce 'noise': send a message while a partner adds random extra flashes/taps, and record which codes still get through and which collapse into nonsense.
Decide, for a given situation (fast message vs noisy channel vs long distance), which code you would choose and justify it against the criteria.
activities.insight: There is no single 'right' code; good codes are judged by trade-offs. Efficient codes give common symbols short patterns, but the BEST solution depends on the criteria — a simple code can beat a fancier one, and a redundant code can survive noise that a flimsy one cannot.

activities.title: Everyday signals and the two-state abstraction
steps: List everyday signals that carry meaning with just two or a few states: traffic lights, thumbs up/down, light on/off, a drum beaten or silent.
For each, state the agreed meaning and who has to share it for the signal to work.
Generalise: pick any two distinguishable things (light/dark, high/low, two symbols) and show they could encode a yes/no answer, or a whole alphabet if you build up patterns.

Connect to real history — telegraph, semaphore, drum signals, computer pixels — and note how each signal travels: seen (e.g. semaphore flags, screen pixels), heard (e.g. drums), or sent as electrical pulses along a wire (the electric telegraph, often heard as clicks at the receiving end).
activities.insight: ANY two distinguishable states, combined into patterns, can represent any message once both sides agree the mapping. 'Patterns transfer information' is a general, everywhere phenomenon, not computer magic, and old and new systems can be compared as solutions to the same problem.

checkQuestion: Two friends want to send messages across a valley using only a torch. One says 'we don't need to plan anything — I'll just flash it and she'll understand.' Will that work? Explain what they actually need for the flashes to carry a message, and whether there's only one correct code they could use.
checkAnswer: No — just flashing doesn't carry a message. Both people must AGREE a code beforehand: a shared system that links particular patterns of flashes to particular meanings (e.g. one flash = yes, two = no, or a flash-pattern per letter). And there is no single 'correct' code — many different codes could do the job, and you compare them on criteria like speed, clarity, and how easy they are to muddle.
